prerequisites: Foundational knowledge from introductory lectures in Chemistry and Physics
Materials Science 1 is required for Materials Science 2

learning_outcomes.text: Students can derive relationships between atomic solid-state structure, microscopic observations, and material characteristic values based on the imparted knowledge of structural and functional materials.
They can apply imparted formulas and solve simple problems.
They are able to read subject-specific diagrams and formulate the result in writing and/or orally.
They can read and interpret material designations and are able to deduce resulting properties and possible uses of the materials.
Students are able to qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate fundamental material science questions independently or in a team and thus apply the theoretically acquired knowledge in practice.
Knowledge of the process chain "manufacturing-microstructure-properties" enables them to familiarize themselves with previously unknown topics in material science.

syllabus_topics: Main material groups, microstructure and properties, material selection
Atomic structure, crystalline and non-crystalline (amorphous) atomic arrangements, lattice defects
Alloy theory
State changes in pure metals, recovery and recrystallization behavior
Material testing
Cyclic deformation behavior, basics of heat treatment, material standards
Important standards for steel and iron
Non-ferrous metals
Polymer materials
Ceramic materials
Composite materials
Knowledge of structural materials and (less extensively) functional materials
Understanding the connections between atomic solid-state structure, microscopic observations, and material characteristic values
Assessment of properties and resulting applications
Properties of various materials based on atomic structure and possible lattice defects
Important phase diagrams, especially the "iron-carbon diagram"
Basic material testing methods: tensile test, hardness test, impact test, fatigue test
Knowledge of possible material damage, e.g., corrosion, and its prevention
Non-destructive material testing methods
Variation of material properties through targeted thermal, thermo-mechanical, and thermo-chemical treatments (focus on steels and latest developments)
Light metals (aluminum, magnesium, titanium and their alloys)
Properties of non-ferrous metals, cemented carbides, shape memory alloys, and ceramic materials
Basic knowledge of magnetic materials, their different properties and applications
assessment_rules: Credits are awarded if the module final examination is passed and qualified participation (a 20-30 minute technical discussion) is demonstrated. The exam requires students to establish connections between structure, properties, and use of materials, name and describe suitable material testing methods, read subject-specific diagrams, extract important values for calculations, perform calculations, describe material science processes, and justify material use for specific applications.
